newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman set to win strong mandate to lead Croatia.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman set to win strong mandate to lead Croatia.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman has widened his lead in his bid for re-election, strenghtening his mandate to push Croatia definitively towards the West, partial results showed on Monday.
With around three-quarters of Sunday's presidential election vote counted, Tudjman had 59.81 percent, placing him far ahead of both opposition candidates.
The latest figure, up from around 57 percent in early counting, virtually assured him of outright victory in the first round, thus eliminating the need for a run-off.
Tudjman, 75, has maintained a high approval rating since leading Croatia to independence from former Yugoslavia in 1991 and steering it through a four-year war against Serbs.
"I expect full results to be even better," Tudjman told reporters after the first results were announced. "The rivals got as much as they promised to people in their programmes.

"I promise the continuity of the policy with which we established Croatian freedom and independence, a stable economy and currency...We are leaving behind the state of war, now we shall dedicate ourselves with all our forces to raising the standards of living for the entire population," he said.

The former general now is in a position to lead Croatia into the 21st century though he has been reported to be suffering from cancer. Unnamed U.S. officials said in November he had been treated for a form of stomach cancer in Washington.

Early results showed that former communist Zdravko Tomac of the Social Democratic party was in second place with 21.96 percent of the votes counted and Vlado Gotovac of the Croatian Social Liberal Party was third with 18.23 percent.
Election officials said the turnout was around 60 percent of the electorate.
Viewed by the West as a key player in the struggling peace process in former Yugoslavia, Tudjman is unlikely to benefit from much of a honeymoon period once in office.
And he will have to weigh the demands of the West against the fears of a public still feeling the effects of war.
Recent unprecedented pressure from the United States and its allies looks set to continue until he tightens up his record on human rights and loosens his grip on the media.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on a visit to the region last month: "We believe that Croatia's future lies in the democratic community we are building. We hold Croatia to the standards of that community, not to the standards of this region's autocratic and violent past."

At a party thrown for his Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) supporters, Tudjman clapped along to chants of "Franjo, Franjo" as supporters crowded round him, waving flags and singing. Fireworks lit up the night sky after early results were announced.
The atmosphere at both opposition headquarters was far more subdued than at Tudjman's celebration.

"There is no food or drink here but the results are above what we expected, especially in the cities. We had a modest campaign but I am sure we'll fare even better in the next election and we'll eventually build a modern democratic Croatia," Tomac told reporters.
Both opposition candidates have already branded the election campaign undemocratic and biased, highlighting attacks on both of them and Tudjman's control of the state media.
Both parties also raised the issue of a low turnout.

"At this moment we failed to incite the feeling that elections matter. A large number of people did not turn out and I think they might have voted for us, because HDZ supporters duly cast their ballots," said Gotovac.

"For the SDP the fight goes on. We have shown that we are continuing to grow. I am sure less people will abstain from voting in next election, which was very worrying," Ivica Racan, Tomac's colleague and leader of the SDP told reporters.

Head of the state electoral commission Ivan Mrkonjic said votes from 6,251 polling stations out of a total of 7,558 had been counted. Votes from soldiers, prisoners and sailors must still be included.
